Se retrouver, se reconnaitre à travers l: Finding each other, recognizing yourself through shared cultural references, taking your place: that's what the improv league La Minorité Risible offers.

J’ai rencontré Kenny Thomas grâce à mon: I met Kenny Thomas through my friend Mara, an improviser with the collective La Minorité Risible. I attended their show last May and played with them at the Impro Momonde at Collège Montmorency, an evening where college players from culturally diverse backgrounds were invited to do improv and step into the spotlight.
Je fais de l’improvisation depuis que j’: I've been doing improv since I was 16, in Montréal and in Saguenay, and I've always been told I was doing a “white people activity.” When I discovered La Minorité Risible, I understood that I could do improv without being any less Latina.
J’étais curieuse de savoir ce qui a moti: I was curious to know what motivated Kenny to found this league and what the players get out of it.
‍<strong>Kenny Thomas est un passionné d: ‍Kenny Thomas is passionate about improv, but he notices a lack of cultural diversity in bar improv leagues in Quebec. To change that, he and his friends founded the leagues Mouvement d’Improvisation Black and La Minorité Risible, spaces where players from visible minorities become the majority.‍
C’est soir de spectacle en ce vendredi 1: It's show night this Friday, July 18. An hour before dusk, we arrive at the theatre La Comédie de Montréal, where improviser Alex Laroche is hosting the improv league La Minorité Risible. Facing the main stage, chairs are set out in rows, ready for an audience that will arrive in about half an hour. An employee directs us to the dressing rooms. A few improvisers are already there, laughing together. About ten minutes later, Kenny Thomas walks in. He is a bald man with tattooed arms, no taller than 1.65 metres, with round tortoiseshell glasses. Everyone stirs, greets him, cracks jokes. He clearly has a way of bringing people together. The league's co-founder sits down on a chair facing a large mirror ringed with yellow bulbs, like the dressing rooms of movie stars.
Kenny grandit dans une famille haïtienne: Kenny grew up in a Haitian family of Jehovah's Witnesses. When he is eight, in the 1990s, his parents buy a property in Montréal-Nord. From that age, he is immersed in the performing arts. Within the walls of his church, a group of mothers, his own among them, gets together once or twice a year to put on plays inspired by the Bible. He puts his hand on his forehead, looking a little discouraged. “The other kids and I, we weren't really down with the idea, to be honest. Doing biblical reenactments, that wasn't hot back then,” he says with a laugh.
D’après ses souvenirs, il a toujours eu: As far as he can remember, he always had this comedic streak, being the one who made everyone else laugh, the “life of the party,” as he puts it, dressed in the official black La Minorité Risible T-shirt. “On all my report cards, [my teachers] wrote: ‘Very intelligent, but very talkative and jokes around with his friends.’”
Kenny se remémore sa première initiation: Kenny recalls his first introduction to improv, in a workshop led by his Grade 5 teacher. “I did one or two improvs, and it was like I'd been doing it my whole life… There was something that let me connect with other people, who weren't necessarily my friends. There was a kind of power in it that I found really stimulating,” he remembers.
Attiré par le théâtre, la littérature et: Drawn to theatre, literature and music, he is the opposite of his brother, who is 14 months older and passionate about sports. His father also had that artistic side. “He missed his calling. He wrote well, was good with his hands and was very eloquent. Everything he did, I felt there was something creative in it,” he says of his father, a welder by training.
À son entrée à l’école secondaire Calixa: When he enters Calixa-Lavallée secondary school, Kenny finds there is no improv team. In Secondary 4, he turns to theatre. “That year, our drama teacher went on burnout leave three months before the end of the year. We put on the play all by ourselves,” he says. The following year, actor Pierre Gendron helps them coordinate a new play and thinks young Kenny could try his luck at the National Theatre School of Canada. “It's rare that at 17, you have something that makes you feel valued, someone who believes in you,” the improviser points out. He lets out a sigh. Under pressure from his mother, he takes a plumbing and heating course, which he drops six months later. Today, Kenny holds a social work diploma from Cégep Marie-Victorin.
Il prend une gorgée d’eau avant de conti: He takes a sip of water before continuing. From 2006 to 2012, he coaches improv for the students of his old secondary school in Montréal-Nord. Among those students are the ones who will give him, in 2008, his first experience in a bar league, first as a referee, then as a player.
L’improvisation est une forme de théâtre: Improv is a form of theatre with no prepared text or material. In an improv match, two teams of six players each compete against each other over 12 timed improvisations. Each improvisation is determined by a card drawn at random that indicates the theme, the number of players allowed, the style (compared or mixed improv), the duration and the category. In Quebec, the Ligue nationale d’improvisation (LNI) is the most important league a player can join, after going through a selection camp.
<strong>« T’as fait beaucoup de personna: “You played a lot of Haitian characters!”
« À l’époque, il y avait tellement peu d: “Back then, there were so few racialized people doing improv in the bar leagues. At some point, you end up knowing everybody!” says Kenny. He says that this minority representation isn't only visual. “Humour is shaped by cultural temperament. The references, what builds the improvs, the ideas in the caucuses, they're often ideas from Quebec's own cultural roots. [...] I realized there was a side of my personality and my identity that I couldn't use in improv because the audience [wouldn't] really get it.”
Le regard tourné vers le sol, Kenny expl: His eyes on the floor, Kenny explains that he wasn't the first to think about creating a new league. Around 2010, through word of mouth, other performers such as Samantha Fins and Richardson Zéphir discussed the idea of building a Black improv league, a project Kenny liked. His gaze lifts to the ceiling, searching for a memory. In 2013, after a match, two of his friends tell him he played a lot of Haitian characters. “But I'm Haitian… what do you mean?” he replies, looking perplexed. “It wasn't meant in a mean way, but at the same time it got me thinking,” Kenny continues. He then asks himself two questions: “When I'm on a stage, what am I playing? Who am I playing for?”
En 2015, il réunit quelques amis pour cr: In 2015, he brings together a few friends to create the Mouvement d’Improvisation Black (MIB). The improviser observes that the league introduces a new audience to the art form: an audience that sees itself in the cultural references on stage. According to Kenny, many of them had never seen improv or theatre before. “Some people would come up to us after the shows and say: ‘That improv, my aunt/my mom does exactly the same thing!’”
Les doigts entrecroisés, Kenny explique: Fingers interlaced, Kenny explains that the project went beyond simply starting a new league: “When we got together, we asked ourselves a lot about what we wanted to bring to the improv world. Did we really want to bring something new? Did we want to play a little with clichés?” he says. He says he doesn't feed stereotypes but laughs at them, so that the audience thinks about what lies underneath these clichés, as his favourite comedian, Dave Chappelle, does. He takes off his glasses and sets them down in front of him. “The idea of the absent father, for example. I said: ‘I know I left, but it was only to go buy milk. The bus didn't come… so I came back home!’” he jokes. At the MIB's second match, a young Haitian woman comes up to him. “Thank you for doing this for us,” she tells him. A sentence that has stayed with him to this day.
La ligue qui se produit ce soir a été cr: The league performing tonight was created in 2023. “The idea is to offer a space where people can see themselves, both those who play and those who come to watch the show,” Kenny explains. The league can welcome all kinds of diversity, not only cultural diversity. In fact, almost no ethnic group, gender or age group is safe from the jokes. “The problem is ignorance of the subject,” he points out. “It's understood that we're going to make fun of everybody a little.” Most members of La Minorité Risible are of Haitian origin, but the co-founder still sees a “diversity within diversity” as he points to his team. “There's a player of Haitian origin who was adopted by a mixed Québécois couple […], and she grew up in the suburbs of Québec City. But she doesn't have the same relationship [with her origins] as I do, having grown up with two Haitian parents in a Montréal context,” he offers as an example.
La Minorité Risible offre un spectacle d: La Minorité Risible puts on a monthly six-player improv show, rather than matches pitting two teams against each other. Photo credit: Ismaël Koné
« C’est un outil pour travailler toutes: “It's a tool for working on all kinds of social skills, creating group dynamics or a sense of belonging. For some people, it's a tool to overcome their shyness or break their isolation,” says Kenny, who has been a youth worker for 25 years. Over the past few years, he has given several improv workshops at various organizations, including a youth centre and a women's shelter.
Alex Laroche coupe son discours, le spec: Alex Laroche cuts himself off; the show is about to start. “That's always what improv has been for me. It's meeting people you don't know, but in one improv, we understood each other!”
« Je n’aurais jamais recommencé à faire: “I never would have started doing improv again if it hadn't been for you,” a La Minorité Risible player tells him. For Kenny, this kind of sentence is “the best reward in the world,” because some members of the league have had negative experiences on their former college teams or elsewhere. “They decide to come back [to improv], to play along, and they find their place.” Today, about fifteen people are part of what Kenny does not hesitate to call his “family.”
